items.question: Who will not eat from the coming sale, according to Elisha?

window_text.1: Elisha replied, “Hear the word of the Lord. This is what the Lord says: About this time tomorrow, a seah of the finest flour will sell for a shekel and two seahs of barley for a shekel at the gate of Samaria.”
window_text.2: The officer on whose arm the king was leaning said to the man of God, “Look, even if the Lord should open the floodgates of the heavens, could this happen?” “You will see it with your own eyes,” answered Elisha, “but you will not eat any of it!”

items.original_question: Who will not eat from the coming sale, according to Elisha?

blind.question: Who will not eat from the coming sale, according to Elisha?

readings.answer: The officer on whose arm the king was leaning
readings.support: The officer on whose arm the king was leaning | but you will not eat any of it!

assessments.reason: The text has the skeptical speaker identified as “the officer on whose arm the king was leaning,” and Elisha replies to him, “You will see it with your own eyes … but you will not eat any of it,” so the officer is the one who will not eat.

blind.reason: Elisha directly tells the officer that although he will see it, he will not eat any of it.

reader.quote: The officer on whose arm the king was leaning said to the man of God, “Look, even if the Lord should open the floodgates of the heavens, could this happen?” “You will see it with your own eyes,” answered Elisha, “but you will not eat any of it!”
reader.contrast: The officer versus the king: Elisha’s second-person “you” refers to the officer who had just challenged the prophecy, not to the king mentioned in the officer’s description.
reader.reason: The dialogue uniquely identifies the officer as the person who will see the event but not eat any of the food. The question is understandable, and answering it requires resolving the addressee of “you.”

editor.quote: The officer on whose arm the king was leaning said to the man of God, “Look, even if the Lord should open the floodgates of the heavens, could this happen?” “You will see it with your own eyes,” answered Elisha, “but you will not eat any of it!”
editor.contrast: The officer versus the king as the person addressed by Elisha’s “you.”
editor.reason: The king is mentioned nearby, so he is a plausible mistaken referent, but Elisha is directly answering the officer’s challenge. The key is therefore unique. However, “eat from the coming sale” is misleading because the officer will not eat the food, not the sale; the stem should ask who will not eat any of the food.

items.question: Which option do the men bring up right after the city?

window_text.3: Now there were four men with leprosy at the entrance of the city gate. They said to each other, “Why stay here until we die?
window_text.4: If we say, ‘We’ll go into the city’—the famine is there, and we will die. And if we stay here, we will die. So let’s go over to the camp of the Arameans and surrender. If they spare us, we live; if they kill us, then we die.”

items.original_question: Which option do the men bring up right after the city?

blind.question: Which option do the men bring up right after the city?

readings.support: And if we stay here, we will die.

assessments.reason: In the speech, after mentioning “We’ll go into the city,” the next option is “And if we stay here,” so “Stay here” matches “staying where they are.”

blind.reason: After “go into the city,” the text immediately says “if we stay here,” establishing that staying where they are is the next option.

reader.quote: And if we stay here, we will die.
reader.contrast: staying where they are versus going to the Arameans’ camp
reader.reason: The stated sequence uniquely places staying there immediately after the option of going into the city. However, “right after the city” is awkward and could sound spatial rather than meaning “right after mentioning going into the city.” The task only requires recalling the order of listed options, not resolving a meaningful relationship.

editor.quote: the famine is there, and we will die. And if we stay here, we will die.
editor.contrast: staying where they are versus going later to the Arameans’ camp
editor.reason: After discussing going into the city, the men next mention staying where they are; going to the Arameans’ camp comes afterward. However, “right after the city” is awkward and could refer to location rather than the order of options. The task mainly tests recall of the options’ sequence, not a consequential relationship.

items.question: Who flees at dusk and leaves the camp behind?
items.competitor: the people who went to the camp

window_text.5: At dusk they got up and went to the camp of the Arameans. When they reached the edge of the camp, no one was there,
window_text.6: for the Lord had caused the Arameans to hear the sound of chariots and horses and a great army, so that they said to one another, “Look, the king of Israel has hired the Hittite and Egyptian kings to attack us!”
window_text.7: So they got up and fled in the dusk and abandoned their tents and their horses and donkeys. They left the camp as it was and ran for their lives.

items.original_question: Who flees at dusk and leaves the camp behind?

blind.question: Who flees at dusk and leaves the camp behind?

readings.support: the Arameans | So they got up and fled in the dusk and abandoned their tents and their horses and donkeys. They left the camp as it was

assessments.reason: Verse 7 says, “So they got up and fled in the dusk and abandoned their tents… They left the camp,” and the antecedent from v6 is “the Arameans,” so the Arameans are the ones who fled and left the camp.

blind.reason: Verse 7, linked to the Arameans in verse 6, states they fled at dusk and left the camp behind.

reader.quote: So they got up and fled in the dusk and abandoned their tents and their horses and donkeys.
reader.contrast: The Arameans, rather than the people who approached their camp, fled and left it behind.
reader.reason: The pronoun “they” in verse 7 refers back to the Arameans in verse 6. Readers must track the change between the people approaching the camp and its occupants fleeing from it.

editor.quote:
the Arameans to hear the sound of chariots and horses and a great army, so that they said to one another, “Look, the king of Israel has hired the Hittite and Egyptian kings to attack us!”
7  So they got up and fled in the dusk
editor.contrast: The fleeing Arameans versus the people who approached the Aramean camp.
editor.reason: The repeated pronoun could initially be confused with the people arriving in verse 5, but the intervening clause identifies the Arameans as those who heard the army, feared an attack, and consequently fled. Resolving that change in pronoun reference is a meaningful actor distinction.

items.question: What do the men plan to report to the royal palace?
items.competitor: The silver, gold, and clothes they hid.

window_text.8: The men who had leprosy reached the edge of the camp, entered one of the tents and ate and drank. Then they took silver, gold and clothes, and went off and hid them. They returned and entered another tent and took some things from it and hid them also.
window_text.9: Then they said to each other, “What we’re doing is not right. This is a day of good news and we are keeping it to ourselves. If we wait until daylight, punishment will overtake us. Let’s go at once and report this to the royal palace.”

items.original_question: What do the men plan to report to the royal palace?

blind.question: What do the men plan to report to the royal palace?

readings.support: This is a day of good news | report this to the royal palace

assessments.reason: The men say, “This is a day of good news” and then, “Let’s go at once and report this to the royal palace,” so the “this” they plan to report is the good news.

blind.reason: The text explicitly ties “this” to “a day of good news,” so they plan to report the good news.

editor.quote: This is a day of good news and we are keeping it to ourselves. If we wait until daylight, punishment will overtake us. Let’s go at once and report this to the royal palace.
editor.contrast: The men intend to report the good news, not the valuables they took and hid.
editor.reason: The alternative is plausible because the valuables are a prominent part of their actions, but they deliberately hide those items. In contrast, “this” in “report this” refers back to the good news they say they should not keep to themselves.

reader.quote: This is a day of good news and we are keeping it to ourselves.
reader.contrast: Whether “this” refers to the good news they are withholding or to the valuables they hid.
reader.reason: The men identify the withheld information as good news and immediately propose reporting it. Nothing indicates that they plan to confess what they hid. The question clearly tests the referent of their planned report.

items.question: What happens after the gatekeepers cry out the report?
items.answer: the news is reported within the palace
items.competitor: the men call out to the gatekeepers

window_text.10: So they went and called out to the city gatekeepers and told them, “We went into the Aramean camp and no one was there—not a sound of anyone—only tethered horses and donkeys, and the tents left just as they were.”
window_text.11: The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was reported within the palace.

items.original_question: What happens after the gatekeepers cry out the report?
items.original_answer: the news is reported within the palace

blind.question: What happens after the gatekeepers cry out the report?

readings.answer: It was reported within the palace.
readings.support: it was reported within the palace

assessments.reason: Verse 11 states directly, “The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was reported within the palace,” matching the answer that it was reported within the palace.

blind.reason: The passage explicitly states the news was reported within the palace after the gatekeepers cried out.

reader.quote: The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was reported within the palace.
reader.contrast: The news being reported within the palace afterward versus the men’s earlier call to the gatekeepers.
reader.reason: The sequence is explicit: after the gatekeepers shout the news, it is reported within the palace. The question tests the order of two related reports rather than merely retrieving an isolated detail.

editor.quote: The gatekeepers shouted the news, and it was reported within the palace.
editor.contrast: The news being reported inside the palace afterward versus the men calling out to the gatekeepers beforehand.
editor.reason: The window explicitly gives the sequence: the men first tell the gatekeepers; then the gatekeepers shout, after which the news is reported within the palace.

items.question: Who plans to take people alive?

window_text.12: The king got up in the night and said to his officers, “I will tell you what the Arameans have done to us. They know we are starving; so they have left the camp to hide in the countryside, thinking, ‘They will surely come out, and then we will take them alive and get into the city.’”
window_text.13: One of his officers answered, “Have some men take five of the horses that are left in the city. Their plight will be like that of all the Israelites left here—yes, they will only be like all these Israelites who are doomed. So let us send them to find out what happened.”

items.original_question: Who plans to take people alive?

blind.question: Who plans to take people alive?

readings.support: the Arameans | we will take them alive

assessments.reason: The king attributes the plan to the Arameans: “they have left the camp… thinking, ‘They will… take them alive.’”

blind.reason: The passage explicitly says the Arameans were thinking they would take them alive.

reader.quote: I will tell you what the Arameans have done to us. They know we are starving; so they have left the camp to hide in the countryside, thinking, ‘They will surely come out, and then we will take them alive and get into the city.’
reader.contrast: The Arameans are the supposed planners; the starving Israelites are the people they intend to take alive.
reader.reason: The king identifies the Arameans as “they,” then voices their supposed thought using “we.” Resolving the nested pronouns distinguishes the actors from their intended captives.

editor.quote: They know we are starving; so they have left the camp to hide in the countryside, thinking, ‘They will surely come out, and then we will take them alive and get into the city.’
editor.contrast: The Arameans are the planners and captors; the starving Israelites are the people they expect to come out and be captured.
editor.reason: The embedded thought is attributed to the Arameans. Resolving “we” as the Arameans and “them” as the Israelites rules out the proposed alternative.

items.question: Who throws away clothing and equipment?

window_text.14: So they selected two chariots with their horses, and the king sent them after the Aramean army. He commanded the drivers, “Go and find out what has happened.”
window_text.15: They followed them as far as the Jordan, and they found the whole road strewn with the clothing and equipment the Arameans had thrown away in their headlong flight. So the messengers returned and reported to the king.
window_text.16: Then the people went out and plundered the camp of the Arameans. So a seah of the finest flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, as the Lord had said.

items.original_question: Who throws away clothing and equipment?

blind.question: Who throws away clothing and equipment?

assessments.reason: Verse 15 states “the clothing and equipment the Arameans had thrown away,” explicitly naming the Arameans as those who threw them away.

blind.reason: The passage explicitly says the Arameans had thrown away the clothing and equipment.

reader.quote: the clothing and equipment the Arameans had thrown away in their headlong flight
reader.contrast: The Arameans discarded the items; the messengers only found them.
reader.reason: The window explicitly identifies the Arameans as the people who threw away the clothing and equipment, distinguishing the actors from the messengers who discovered the abandoned items.

editor.quote: the clothing and equipment the Arameans had thrown away
editor.contrast: The Arameans threw the items away; the messengers found them and reported back.
editor.reason: The question tests which group performed the act of discarding, rather than confusing them with the group that discovered the discarded items.

items.question: Who did the people trample to death?
items.answer: the officer the king put in charge of the gate

window_text.17: Now the king had put the officer on whose arm he leaned in charge of the gate, and the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died, just as the man of God had foretold when the king came down to his house.
window_text.18: It happened as the man of God had said to the king: “About this time tomorrow, a seah of the finest flour will sell for a shekel and two seahs of barley for a shekel at the gate of Samaria.”

items.original_question: Who did the people trample to death?
items.original_answer: the officer the king put in charge of the gate

blind.question: Who did the people trample to death?

readings.answer: The officer on whose arm the king leaned
readings.support: the officer on whose arm he leaned | the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died

assessments.reason: The verse states the king put “the officer on whose arm he leaned” in charge of the gate, and that he was trampled and died; this matches the key’s identification.

blind.reason: The text directly identifies the trampled person as the officer the king leaned on and had put in charge of the gate.

reader.quote: the king had put the officer on whose arm he leaned in charge of the gate, and the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died
reader.contrast: The officer was trampled; the king was not.
reader.reason: The pronoun “him” refers to the officer whom the king placed at the gate. The reader must distinguish the victim from the king who appointed him.

editor.quote: the king had put the officer on whose arm he leaned in charge of the gate, and the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died
editor.contrast: The officer was trampled; the king was the person who had assigned him to the gate.
editor.reason: The reader must resolve “him” as referring to the officer rather than the nearby king. The sentence’s structure keeps the officer as the person at the gate who was trampled and died.

items.question: Whose words come true about the officer?

window_text.19: The officer had said to the man of God, “Look, even if the Lord should open the floodgates of the heavens, could this happen?” The man of God had replied, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it!”
window_text.20: And that is exactly what happened to him, for the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died.

items.original_question: Whose words come true about the officer?

blind.question: Whose words come true about the officer?

readings.support: The man of God had replied | And that is exactly what happened to him

assessments.reason: The passage recounts the man of God’s prediction and then says it happened exactly so, showing his words came true.

blind.reason: The text explicitly says what the man of God said and that it happened exactly as he said.

reader.quote: The man of God had replied, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it!”
reader.contrast: The man of God’s prediction versus the officer’s skeptical question.
reader.reason: “That is exactly what happened” refers to the predicted fate of the officer: he would witness the event but not partake of it. The officer’s own words merely questioned whether the event could happen.

editor.quote: “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it!”
editor.contrast: The reader must distinguish the officer’s skeptical question from the man of God’s prediction about what the officer would experience.
editor.reason: The officer merely questions whether the event could happen. The man of God predicts that the officer will see it but not eat any of it, and verse 20 explicitly says that this is exactly what happened to him.

duplicate_judgments.reason: Both identify the Arameans as the people who fled and abandoned or discarded their belongings. v5-7:1 is preferable because it directly tests the central event—the Arameans fleeing at dusk and leaving the camp—while v14-16:1 asks about a narrower trace of that same flight, the discarded clothing and equipment.
